OPA - Oil Pollution Act.q: Oil spills on deck during bunkering. What should be done first?
options: Stop the transfer, raise the alarm and follow the response plan
Wash the oil overboard with fire hoses
Cover the spill and say nothing
OPA - Oil Pollution Act.why: Stopping the source and starting the response plan limits the amount of oil spilled.

OPA - Oil Pollution Act.q: Why are deck scuppers plugged before oil transfer operations?
options: To keep spilled oil on deck from going overboard
To improve ventilation of cargo tanks
To stop crew slipping on deck
OPA - Oil Pollution Act.why: Plugged scuppers contain any spill on deck so it can be cleaned up before reaching the sea.

OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.q: How should a wrong entry in a logbook be corrected?
options: Erase it and write over it
Strike it through with a single line, write the correct entry and sign
OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.why: A single line keeps the original readable, which preserves the logbook as a reliable legal record.

OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.q: When should logbook entries be made?
options: At the end of the voyage
At the time of the event or as soon as possible after
OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.why: Entries made at or near the time are more accurate and are accepted as reliable evidence.

OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.q: What should be used to write entries in an official logbook?
options: Pencil, so it can be corrected
OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.why: Permanent ink prevents entries from being changed or erased.

OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.q: The pages of an official logbook should:
options: Be removed if they contain mistakes
Be rewritten neatly at the end of each month
OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.why: Numbered pages that are never removed show that the record is complete and has not been altered.

OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.q: Who normally signs the deck logbook entries for a navigational watch?
OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.why: The officer of the watch is responsible for the entries made during his watch and signs them.

options: They are personal diaries of the officers
They are legal records used as evidence in inspections and investigations
They are only used for crew training
OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.why: Logbooks are official records that authorities, courts and investigators rely on.

OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.q: Under SOLAS, what must be recorded in the log-book about emergency drills?
options: Nothing, drills need not be recorded
Drills, training and inspections of life-saving appliances
Only fire drills held in port
OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.why: SOLAS Chapter III requires musters, drills, training and inspections to be recorded in the log-book.

OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.q: A good logbook entry should be:
options: Factual and clear, with times and details
Written later from memory at month's end
As short as possible, without times
OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.why: Factual, timed and detailed entries are useful and credible records of what happened.

OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.q: Which information is typically recorded in the engine room logbook?
options: Main engine RPM, temperatures, pressures and fuel use
OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.why: The engine logbook records machinery operation and performance data.

OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.q: Why must the time used (ship's time or UTC) be clear in log entries?
options: To make the page look tidy
So crew know when meals are served
So events can be accurately timed and compared with other records
Because port authorities read only UTC
OPESLOG - Orientation on Proper Entries.why: Clear times allow events to be placed in order and matched with records such as the VDR and engine log.

ORB - Oil Record Book.q: The Oil Record Book is required under:
ORB - Oil Record Book.why: MARPOL Annex I, which covers oil pollution, requires ships to keep an Oil Record Book.

ORB - Oil Record Book.q: Oil Record Book Part II is required for:
options: All ships of 400 GT and above
Oil tankers of 150 GT and above, for cargo and ballast operations
ORB - Oil Record Book.why: Part II records cargo and ballast operations and is required on oil tankers of 150 GT and above.

ORB - Oil Record Book.q: Oil Record Book Part I (machinery space operations) is required on every ship, other than an oil tanker, of:
ORB - Oil Record Book.why: MARPOL Annex I requires ORB Part I on oil tankers of 150 GT and above and other ships of 400 GT and above.

ORB - Oil Record Book.q: How long must the Oil Record Book be kept on board after the last entry?
ORB - Oil Record Book.why: MARPOL requires the Oil Record Book to be kept readily available for three years after the last entry.

ORB - Oil Record Book.q: Who signs the Oil Record Book entries?
options: Each operation by the officer in charge, and each completed page by the master
Only the chief engineer, once at the end of each voyage
Only the port State inspector during inspection
Only the company superintendent every month
ORB - Oil Record Book.why: MARPOL requires each operation to be signed by the officer in charge and each completed page by the master.

ORB - Oil Record Book.q: When sludge is delivered to a port reception facility, what should the ship keep as supporting evidence?
options: Only a verbal confirmation from the agent
A photo of the receiving truck
Nothing, since the ORB entry is enough
The receipt or certificate issued by the reception facility
ORB - Oil Record Book.why: The reception facility receipt supports the ORB entry and proves the sludge was properly disposed of.

ORB - Oil Record Book.q: In ORB Part I, bunkering of fuel or bulk lubricating oil is recorded under:
ORB - Oil Record Book.why: Code H is used for bunkering of fuel or bulk lubricating oil.

ORB - Oil Record Book.q: Machinery space bilge water discharged through the oily water separator must have an oil content not exceeding:
ORB - Oil Record Book.why: MARPOL Annex I limits the oil content of discharged machinery space bilge water to 15 ppm.

ORB - Oil Record Book.q: An accidental or other exceptional discharge of oil is recorded in ORB Part I under:
ORB - Oil Record Book.why: Code G is used for accidental or other exceptional discharges of oil.

ORB - Oil Record Book.q: If the Oil Record Book is written in the flag State's official language, a ship holding an IOPP Certificate must also make entries in:
ORB - Oil Record Book.why: MARPOL requires entries in English, French or Spanish as well when the flag language is different, for ships holding an IOPP Certificate.

PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.q: How does alcohol affect a seafarer on duty?
options: It slows reactions and impairs judgement
PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.why: Alcohol slows the brain, reducing reaction speed, coordination and decision-making.

PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.q: Under STCW, the alcohol limit for seafarers performing safety, security and environmental duties is no more than:
options: 0.10% blood alcohol or 0.50 mg/l in breath
0.20% blood alcohol or 1.0 mg/l in breath
0.05% blood alcohol or 0.25 mg/l in breath
0.08% blood alcohol or 0.40 mg/l in breath
PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.why: STCW Code Section A-VIII/1 sets a limit of 0.05% blood alcohol or 0.25 mg/l in breath.

options: Free from the effects of alcohol, drugs and fatigue that could affect safe work
Having finished breakfast before the watch
PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.why: Fitness for duty means being in a condition to perform tasks safely, without impairment.

PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.q: You suspect a crewmate is under the influence of alcohol while on watch. What should you do?
options: Cover his duties without telling anyone
Give him coffee and let him continue
Ignore it unless an accident happens
Report it to the officer in charge or the master
PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.why: An impaired person on duty endangers the ship, so it must be reported so action can be taken.

PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.q: A typical company drug and alcohol policy includes:
options: Rules that apply to officers only
PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.why: Random and for-cause testing helps deter and detect substance misuse among all crew.

PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.q: A seafarer is taking prescribed medicine that may cause drowsiness. What should he do?
options: Inform the master or responsible officer before going on duty
PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.why: Some medicines impair alertness, so the officer must know in order to decide whether duties are safe.

PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.q: Which signs may suggest alcohol or drug misuse?
options: Slurred speech, unsteady walking and frequent lateness
A neat uniform and good punctuality
PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.why: Slurred speech, poor balance and repeated lateness are common signs of impairment.

PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.q: What is the only reliable way to remove alcohol from the body?
options: Giving the body time to break it down
PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.why: The liver removes alcohol at a fixed rate, and coffee, showers or exercise do not speed it up.

PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.q: A seafarer realizes he has a drinking problem. What should he do?
options: Keep it secret until the end of contract
Seek help early through company support or medical channels
PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.why: Seeking help early allows treatment and support before the problem causes an accident or job loss.

PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.q: What is a likely consequence of being found drunk on duty?
PADAMS - Prevention of Alcohol and Drug.why: Being impaired on duty breaks company policy and safety rules, leading to discipline or dismissal.

PAMA - Paint Maintenance.q: What is the most important factor for a long-lasting paint coating?
options: The time of day it is applied
PAMA - Paint Maintenance.why: Most coating failures are caused by poor surface preparation, so it matters most for coating life.

PAMA - Paint Maintenance.q: Before painting a rusty steel surface, the crew should first:
options: Paint directly over the loose rust
Remove loose rust, scale and dirt, then clean the surface
PAMA - Paint Maintenance.why: Paint only sticks well to a clean, sound surface free of loose rust, salt and dirt.

PAMA - Paint Maintenance.q: What is the main purpose of a primer coat?
options: To make the paint dry faster in rain
To improve adhesion and protect steel from corrosion
To replace the need for a topcoat
PAMA - Paint Maintenance.why: Primer bonds to the steel, helps later coats stick and provides corrosion protection.

PAMA - Paint Maintenance.q: Paint should not be applied when the steel surface temperature is less than how much above the dew point?
PAMA - Paint Maintenance.why: The common rule is at least 3°C above dew point, so moisture does not condense on the surface under the paint.

PAMA - Paint Maintenance.q: When painting inside an enclosed or poorly ventilated space, you should:
options: Close all openings to keep the smell inside
Provide good ventilation and wear suitable respiratory protection
PAMA - Paint Maintenance.why: Paint fumes can be toxic and flammable, so ventilation and respiratory protection are essential.

PAMA - Paint Maintenance.q: Where should paint and thinners be stored on board?
options: In the designated paint locker with fire protection
PAMA - Paint Maintenance.why: Paints and thinners are flammable and must be kept in the designated paint store with fire protection.

PAMA - Paint Maintenance.q: Which tool checks the paint thickness while it is still wet?
PAMA - Paint Maintenance.why: A wet film thickness comb gauge measures thickness right after application so it can be corrected.

PAMA - Paint Maintenance.q: Steel on ships rusts mainly because of contact with:
PAMA - Paint Maintenance.why: Corrosion needs oxygen and water, and salt in seawater makes it happen faster.

PAMA - Paint Maintenance.q: Why must sacrificial zinc anodes on the hull be left unpainted?
options: Paint stops them from giving cathodic protection
Paint makes the hull rust faster
PAMA - Paint Maintenance.why: Anodes protect the hull by corroding in place of the steel, and paint would stop this from working.

PAMA - Paint Maintenance.q: Which PPE is most important when spray painting?
options: A life jacket and a safety helmet
Safety shoes and a sun hat
Ear muffs and a safety harness
A respirator, goggles, gloves and coveralls
PAMA - Paint Maintenance.why: Spray mist can be inhaled and can harm the eyes and skin, so respiratory, eye and skin protection is needed.

PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.q: Under the ISPS Code, before entering a port the ship may be required to give the port State:
options: Security information such as its ISSC and security level
PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.why: The ISPS Code allows port States to request security information before a ship enters port.

PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.q: Why are the main engine tested astern and the steering gear checked before entering port?
options: To be sure they are ready for maneuvering in confined waters
PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.why: Port approaches need reliable astern power and steering, so they are tested before entering confined waters.

PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.q: Who should supervise the rigging of the pilot ladder and the boarding of the pilot?
options: A responsible officer in contact with the bridge
Nobody, as the pilot handles it
PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.why: SOLAS requires pilot boarding to be supervised by a responsible officer who can communicate with the bridge.

PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.q: When the pilot boards, the master and pilot should:
options: Exchange information on the passage plan and ship's maneuvering characteristics
PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.why: The master-pilot information exchange makes sure both share the same plan and know the ship's handling.

PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.q: During the port approach, the anchors should be:
options: Cleared away and ready for immediate use
PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.why: Anchors ready for use can stop the ship in an emergency such as engine or steering failure.

PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.q: Which document is normally prepared for port clearance on arrival?
PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.why: Port authorities, immigration and agents require the crew list for arrival clearance.

PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.q: During mooring operations, crew should avoid standing in:
options: Snap-back zones of mooring lines under tension
PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.why: A parted mooring line can recoil with great force and seriously injure anyone in the snap-back zone.

PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.q: When entering a Vessel Traffic Service (VTS) area, the ship should:
options: Switch off the VHF to avoid noise
Make the required reports and listen on the assigned VHF channel
PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.why: VTS reporting and listening watch help the shore station manage traffic and warn of dangers.

PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.q: Before entering an Emission Control Area, the engine department must:
options: Switch off the oily water separator alarm
Change over to compliant fuel and record it
PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.why: MARPOL Annex VI requires compliant fuel in ECAs and a record of the fuel changeover.

PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.q: What is the purpose of a pre-arrival checklist?
options: To make sure all safety and operational items are checked
PAP - Preparation of Arrival in Port.why: Checklists under the ISM system make sure important steps are not forgotten before arrival.

PDS - Practical Deck Skill.q: Which knot makes a fixed loop at the end of a rope that will not slip?
PDS - Practical Deck Skill.why: The bowline forms a secure loop that does not slip or jam under load.

PDS - Practical Deck Skill.q: Which knot is used to join two ropes of different sizes?
options: Round turn and two half hitches
PDS - Practical Deck Skill.why: The sheet bend joins ropes of different thickness securely.

PDS - Practical Deck Skill.q: Which knot is used as a stopper to prevent a rope running out through a block?
PDS - Practical Deck Skill.why: The figure of eight knot makes a bulky stopper at the end of a rope.

PDS - Practical Deck Skill.q: Which knot joins two ropes of the same size, such as when tying a bundle?
PDS - Practical Deck Skill.why: The reef knot joins two ends of equal size and is used for tying bundles and reefing.

PDS - Practical Deck Skill.q: What is the purpose of whipping a rope's end?
options: To stop the end of the rope from fraying
PDS - Practical Deck Skill.why: Whipping binds the strands at the rope's end so they do not unravel.

options: The area where a mooring line may recoil if it parts
A rest area for the crew
PDS - Practical Deck Skill.why: If a line under tension breaks, it whips back violently through the snap-back zone.

PDS - Practical Deck Skill.q: During mooring, why should crew never stand inside a bight (loop) of rope?
options: The rope can suddenly tighten and trap or injure them
PDS - Practical Deck Skill.why: A bight can close quickly under load and catch a person's leg or body.

PDS - Practical Deck Skill.q: A right-hand laid rope should normally be coiled:
PDS - Practical Deck Skill.why: Coiling right-hand laid rope clockwise follows its lay and prevents kinks.

PDS - Practical Deck Skill.q: Before using a chipping hammer or grinder on deck, a seaman should:
options: Check the tool and wear goggles, gloves and ear protection
Remove the safety guard to work faster
Start work without telling the bosun
Use it in the rain with bare hands
PDS - Practical Deck Skill.why: Checking the tool and wearing PPE protects against flying particles, noise and tool failure.

PDS - Practical Deck Skill.q: When working aloft, a seaman must:
options: Wear a safety harness attached to a strong point
Carry tools loose in his pockets
Drop tools to the deck after use
PDS - Practical Deck Skill.why: A harness secured to a strong point prevents a fatal fall from height.

options: Taking responsibility for your actions and their results
PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.why: Accountability means owning your actions and their results, good or bad.

PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.q: When working with a multinational crew, the best approach is to:
options: Respect cultural differences and use the ship's common working language
PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.why: Respect and a common working language reduce misunderstandings and build teamwork.

PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.q: Which is an example of professionalism on board?
options: Using a mobile phone while on lookout
Arriving on time, rested and ready for duty
Leaving the watch before relief arrives
PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.why: Being punctual, rested and prepared shows respect for the job and the team.

PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.q: A port official asks you for an unofficial payment. What is the correct action?
options: Pay it quickly from your own money
Refuse politely and report to the master according to company policy
PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.why: Ethical conduct means refusing bribes and following company anti-corruption procedures.

options: Planning your tasks and rest time well
Leaving tasks until the last minute
PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.why: Planning work and rest keeps you productive and fit for duty.

PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.q: What does discipline mean in the workplace?
options: Following rules only when an officer is watching
Following rules and procedures even when no one is watching
PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.why: True discipline is consistent good conduct whether or not someone is supervising.

options: Looking at your phone while others speak
Giving full attention and asking questions to understand
Planning your reply while others talk
PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.why: Active listening means focusing on the speaker and checking your understanding.

PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.q: Good feedback to a crewmate should be:
options: Specific, polite and about the behaviour, not the person
PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.why: Specific, respectful feedback focused on behaviour helps people improve without feeling attacked.

PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.q: A seafarer with strong team spirit will:
options: Do only his own task and nothing else
Compete to make others look bad
Help teammates and share useful information
PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.why: Helping others and sharing information makes the whole team safer and more effective.

options: Following the majority even if they are wrong
Telling people what they want to hear
Being honest and doing what is right consistently
Being loyal only to close friends
PEVF - Personal Effectiveness and Values.why: Integrity is being honest and acting rightly at all times.

PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.q: Before launching the fast rescue boat, the coxswain must make sure the crew:
options: Wear immersion suits or lifejackets and helmets as required
Remove their boots to swim better
PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.why: Proper protective equipment protects the crew from cold water, impact and drowning.

PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.q: Under the LSA Code, a fast rescue boat with a crew of three must be able to reach a calm-water speed of at least:
PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.why: The LSA Code requires fast rescue boats to maneuver at 20 knots or more with a crew of three.

PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.q: When launching a fast rescue boat from a ship that is making way, the painter is used to:
options: Tow the boat behind the ship at full speed
Lift the boat back on board
Keep the boat in position alongside and stop it swinging aft
Secure a casualty in the water
PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.why: The painter holds the boat in position alongside so it can be released and steered away safely.

PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.q: When approaching a person in the water, the coxswain should normally:
options: Approach at full speed from upwind
Circle the person at high speed
Approach slowly, heading into the wind and sea
PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.why: A slow approach into the wind and sea gives better control and avoids drifting onto the person.

PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.q: How should a casualty suspected of hypothermia be lifted from the water?
options: Horizontally, if possible, to reduce the risk of collapse
Vertically by the arms, as fast as possible
By letting the casualty climb in alone
By towing the casualty to the ship
PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.why: A horizontal lift reduces the sudden drop in blood pressure that can cause collapse after rescue.

PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.q: What is the purpose of the engine kill cord (cut-off lanyard)?
options: To stop the engine if the coxswain is thrown from the helm
To switch on the navigation lights
PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.why: The kill cord stops the engine so a runaway boat cannot injure people in the water.

PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.q: If the fast rescue boat capsizes, the crew should first:
options: Account for all crew and stay with the boat
Swim away from the boat separately
PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.why: Staying together with the boat makes the crew easier to find and gives them something to hold.

PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.q: To reduce injury from wave slamming at high speed, crew should:
options: Sit on the side tubes without holding on
Hold on firmly and flex the knees to absorb shocks
PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.why: Firm handholds and bent knees absorb impacts and reduce back and leg injuries.

PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.q: How should the coxswain keep in contact with the ship during the rescue?
PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.why: Portable VHF gives reliable two-way communication between the boat and the ship.

PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.q: During recovery, the boat should be hooked onto the davit fall when:
options: It is under the davit, held by the painter and moving with the ship
It is still moving at full speed
The crew have left the boat
PFRBC - Proficiency in Fast Rescue Boat.why: Hooking on while held steady under the davit by the painter prevents dangerous swinging and shock loads.

PP - Passage Planning.q: What is the correct order of the four stages of passage planning?
PP - Passage Planning.why: IMO guidelines describe passage planning as appraisal, planning, execution and monitoring.

PP - Passage Planning.q: Which SOLAS chapter requires voyage planning before a ship goes to sea?
PP - Passage Planning.why: SOLAS Chapter V on safety of navigation requires the master to plan the voyage before departure.

PP - Passage Planning.q: What is done in the appraisal stage?
options: Gathering all information relevant to the voyage
Comparing actual position with the plan
PP - Passage Planning.why: Appraisal collects charts, publications, weather, tides and other information needed to plan.

PP - Passage Planning.q: Charts and publications used for the passage plan must be corrected using:
PP - Passage Planning.why: Notices to Mariners provide the corrections that keep charts and publications up to date.

options: Height of the mast above the water
Distance between the keel and the seabed
Distance between the ship and the berth
PP - Passage Planning.why: UKC is the depth of water under the keel and must stay above the safe minimum.

PP - Passage Planning.q: In a passage plan, 'no-go areas' are:
options: Areas where the ship must not go because of insufficient depth or other dangers
Areas of the ship closed to crew
PP - Passage Planning.why: No-go areas are marked on the chart so the navigator keeps the ship clear of danger.

options: The point where the pilot boards
The point where the rudder is put over to start a course alteration
The point where the anchor is dropped
PP - Passage Planning.why: The wheel-over point allows for the ship's turning so it settles on the new track as planned.

options: A way of filing charts in folders
A radar technique to monitor the ship's distance off the planned track
PP - Passage Planning.why: Parallel indexing uses a fixed radar target to show at a glance if the ship is drifting off track.

PP - Passage Planning.q: What is an abort point in a passage plan?
options: The point where the voyage ends
The last point at which the ship can safely abandon the maneuver or turn back
A place to stop for fishing
PP - Passage Planning.why: Beyond the abort point the ship is committed, so the decision to continue must be made before it.

PP - Passage Planning.q: Before the voyage begins, the passage plan should be:
options: Approved by the master and briefed to the bridge team
Kept private by the second officer
PP - Passage Planning.why: The master approves the plan and all watchkeepers must know it before the voyage starts.

PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.q: Where does PPE stand in the hierarchy of controls?
options: The last line of defence after other controls
Not needed if the worker is trained
PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.why: PPE only protects the wearer and is used when hazards cannot be eliminated or controlled in other ways.

PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.q: If a safety helmet has a crack in the shell, you should:
options: Replace it with a sound helmet
PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.why: A cracked helmet cannot absorb impact properly and must be replaced.

PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.q: Which PPE should be worn in a noisy engine room?
PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.why: Hearing protection prevents noise-induced hearing loss in high-noise areas.

PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.q: A full-body safety harness is required when:
options: Working aloft or over the side
PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.why: A harness protects against falls when working at height or over the side.

PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.q: PPE should be selected based on:
options: The hazards identified in the risk assessment
PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.why: PPE must match the actual hazards of the task, as identified by risk assessment.

PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.q: When handling corrosive chemicals, the correct gloves are:
options: Chemical-resistant gloves as stated in the SDS
PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.why: Only gloves made of a material resistant to that chemical, as shown in the SDS, protect the skin.

PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.q: When chipping rust or grinding, which PPE protects the eyes best?
options: Safety goggles or a face shield
PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.why: Safety goggles or a face shield are designed to stop flying particles from hitting the eyes.

PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.q: Which statement about PPE is correct?
options: PPE reduces exposure but does not remove the hazard
One type of PPE suits all tasks
PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.why: PPE only reduces exposure, which is why its limits must be understood.

PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.q: Before each use, PPE should be:
options: Inspected for damage and correct condition
PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.why: Damaged PPE may fail when needed, so it must be checked before every use.

PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.q: Safety shoes with steel toe caps protect against:
options: Falling objects and crushing injuries to the feet
PPE - Personal Protective Equipment.why: Steel toe caps protect the toes from heavy falling or rolling objects.

PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.q: What is the general emergency alarm signal on board?
options: Seven or more short blasts followed by one long blast
PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.why: SOLAS defines the general emergency alarm as seven or more short blasts followed by one long blast.

PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.q: What does the muster list show?
options: Each person's emergency duties and muster station
PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.why: The muster list tells each person where to go and what to do in an emergency.

PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.q: You see someone fall overboard. What should you do first?
options: Jump in to rescue the person
Run to your cabin for help
Shout 'man overboard', throw a lifebuoy and keep pointing at the person
Wait for someone else to act
PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.why: Raising the alarm, giving flotation and keeping sight of the person are the critical first actions.

PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.q: Before entering an enclosed space, you must:
options: Enter quickly and come out fast
Wait until the ship reaches port
Have a permit and confirm the atmosphere is tested safe
PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.why: Enclosed spaces can lack oxygen or contain toxic gas, so a permit and atmosphere testing are required.

PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.q: Where is smoking allowed on board?
PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.why: Smoking only in designated areas reduces the risk of fire.
The fire triangle shows that fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen, and removing one puts it out.

PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.q: Why must loose objects be secured on board?
options: Ship motion can make them move and cause injury
PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.why: Rolling and pitching can turn unsecured objects into dangerous moving hazards.

PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.q: New crew members must receive safety familiarization:
options: Only if they ask for it
At the end of their contract
PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.why: STCW requires safety familiarization before a new seafarer is assigned duties on board.

PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.q: Who gives the order to abandon ship?
options: Any crew member who feels unsafe
PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.why: Only the master gives the order to abandon ship.

PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.q: You notice a damaged handrail on deck. What should you do?
options: Ignore it if it is not in your area
Wait for the next safety meeting
Report it to the officer in charge immediately
Fix it quietly without telling anyone
PSA - Personal Safety Awareness.why: Reporting hazards at once allows them to be controlled before someone is hurt.

PSC - Port State Control.q: What is the main purpose of port State control?
options: To collect port fees from foreign ships
To check that foreign ships comply with international conventions
To issue ships' certificates for the flag State
PSC - Port State Control.why: PSC is a second line of defence that verifies foreign ships meet international safety, pollution and labour standards.

PSC - Port State Control.q: The Philippines is a member of which regional port State control agreement?
PSC - Port State Control.why: The Tokyo MOU covers the Asia-Pacific region, and the Philippines is a member.

PSC - Port State Control.q: A PSC inspection usually begins with:
options: Checking the ship's certificates and documents
PSC - Port State Control.why: The initial inspection starts by checking certificates and documents, followed by a general look at the ship.

PSC - Port State Control.q: A more detailed PSC inspection is carried out when there are:
options: Valid certificates and a clean ship
Clear grounds that the ship or crew do not meet requirements
PSC - Port State Control.why: Clear grounds, such as invalid certificates or visible deficiencies, justify a more detailed inspection.

PSC - Port State Control.q: What does detention by port State control mean?
options: The ship cannot sail until serious deficiencies are fixed
PSC - Port State Control.why: A detained ship is held in port until the deficiencies that make it unsafe are corrected.

PSC - Port State Control.q: Which area is among the most common sources of PSC deficiencies?
options: The font of the ship's name
PSC - Port State Control.why: Fire safety and life-saving appliances are consistently among the top deficiency areas in PSC reports.

PSC - Port State Control.q: When a PSC officer records a deficiency, the ship should:
options: Ignore it until the next drydock
Correct it within the agreed time and keep evidence of the repair
PSC - Port State Control.why: Deficiencies must be rectified as required, with records kept to show they were fixed.

PSC - Port State Control.q: During a PSC inspection, crew may be asked to:
options: Cook a meal for the inspector
Demonstrate a fire or abandon ship drill
PSC - Port State Control.why: PSC officers may check operational readiness by asking the crew to carry out drills.

PSC - Port State Control.q: What is the best way to prepare for a PSC inspection?
options: Prepare only when the inspector arrives
Keep certificates valid, records updated and equipment maintained at all times
PSC - Port State Control.why: Continuous compliance is the only reliable way to pass PSC inspections.

PSC - Port State Control.q: Under risk-based inspection regimes such as that of the Tokyo MOU, ships with a high-risk profile are:
options: Inspected only once in their life
PSC - Port State Control.why: Risk-based regimes target high-risk ships with more frequent inspections.

options: Anything with the potential to cause harm
The chance that harm will happen
RAC - Risk Assessment Course.why: A hazard is a source of potential harm, while risk is how likely and how serious that harm is.
Risk is rated by how likely harm is to happen and how severe it would be.

RAC - Risk Assessment Course.q: Which is the correct order of the hierarchy of controls, from most to least effective?
RAC - Risk Assessment Course.why: Removing or replacing the hazard is most effective, and PPE is the last line of defence.

RAC - Risk Assessment Course.q: When should a task-based risk assessment be done?
options: Once a year by the office
Before the task starts, involving the people who will do it
RAC - Risk Assessment Course.why: Assessing before work with the people involved finds the real hazards and agrees controls in advance.

RAC - Risk Assessment Course.q: Installing a guard on a rotating machine is an example of:
RAC - Risk Assessment Course.why: A guard is a physical barrier between people and the hazard, which is an engineering control.

RAC - Risk Assessment Course.q: Which is an example of an administrative control?
RAC - Risk Assessment Course.why: Permits, procedures and training control risk by changing how people work.

options: Risk left after control measures are applied
Risk that has been fully removed
RAC - Risk Assessment Course.why: Residual risk is what remains after controls and must be acceptable before work starts.

RAC - Risk Assessment Course.q: A risk assessment should be reviewed when:
options: Only when port State control asks
Work conditions change or after an incident
RAC - Risk Assessment Course.why: Changes and incidents can create new hazards, so the assessment must be updated.

RAC - Risk Assessment Course.q: A toolbox talk is used to:
options: Brief the work team on hazards and controls before the job
RAC - Risk Assessment Course.why: A toolbox talk makes sure everyone understands the hazards and safe-work requirements before starting.

RAC - Risk Assessment Course.q: If a task is assessed as high risk, the team should:
options: Not start until further controls reduce the risk
Do it without telling the officer
RAC - Risk Assessment Course.why: High-risk work must not proceed until additional controls bring the risk to an acceptable level.

RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.q: How does radar measure the range of a target?
options: By measuring the time for a pulse to return from the target
By measuring the colour of the target
By listening for the target's whistle
RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.why: Radar times how long a pulse takes to travel to the target and back, then converts it to distance.

RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.q: What does the gain control adjust?
options: The colour of the range rings
RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.why: Gain controls receiver sensitivity, which affects how strongly echoes appear on the display.

RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.q: The sea clutter control (STC) is used to reduce:
options: Echoes from waves close to the ship
RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.why: Sea clutter control reduces strong wave echoes near the centre of the display.

RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.q: Which control is used to reduce echoes caused by rain?
RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.why: The rain clutter control (FTC) reduces the large echoes produced by rain and snow.

RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.q: The Variable Range Marker (VRM) is used to measure:
RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.why: The VRM is a ring that can be adjusted to measure the distance to a target.

RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.q: Compared with X-band radar, S-band radar is better at:
options: Showing small targets in sharp detail
Detecting targets in heavy rain and sea clutter
RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.why: The longer wavelength of S-band is less affected by rain and sea clutter.

RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.q: Blind or shadow sectors on a radar display are mainly caused by:
options: Masts, funnels and other structures blocking the beam
RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.why: Ship structures near the scanner block the beam, creating sectors where targets may not be seen.

RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.q: In a North-up display, the top of the screen represents:
RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.why: In North-up mode the display is stabilized by the gyro so that north is always at the top.

RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.q: Which target is most likely to be missed by radar?
options: A small wooden or fibreglass boat in rough sea
A steel buoy with a radar reflector
RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.why: Small non-metal boats give weak echoes that are easily lost in sea clutter.

RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.q: Multiple echoes appearing at two and three times the range of a close target are caused by:
options: Repeated reflections between own ship and the target
RADAROC - RADAR Operation Course.why: The pulse bounces back and forth between own ship and a large close target, creating evenly spaced false echoes.

RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.q: What is the main purpose of an incident investigation?
options: To find root causes and prevent recurrence
RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.why: Investigations aim to learn why the incident happened so it does not happen again.

RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.q: Which section of the ISM Code covers reports and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences?
RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.why: ISM Code Section 9 requires these events to be reported, investigated and analysed.

options: The basic underlying reason that, if corrected, prevents recurrence
The last action before the accident
The person nearest to the accident
RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.why: Fixing the root cause, not just the immediate cause, stops similar incidents from happening.

RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.q: After a serious incident, why should the VDR data be saved promptly?
options: To clear space for new voyages
Because the recording may be overwritten after some time
RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.why: The VDR records in a loop, so data must be saved before it is overwritten.

options: Asking 'why' repeatedly to find the root cause
RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.why: Repeatedly asking 'why' digs past symptoms to the underlying cause.

options: Together in a group so stories match
As soon as possible, one at a time, in a calm and non-blaming way
RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.why: Early, separate and non-blaming interviews give more accurate and honest accounts.

RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.q: A good corrective action should be:
options: Specific, measurable, assigned to someone and given a deadline
RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.why: Specific, measurable and assigned actions can be tracked and checked for effectiveness.

RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.q: A crew member slips on an oily deck caused by a leak left unrepaired for weeks. The oily deck is the:
RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.why: The oily deck directly caused the slip, while the failure to repair the leak is closer to the root cause.

RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.q: Why are near misses investigated as well as accidents?
options: They are required only on passenger ships
They show hazards that could cause serious accidents next time
RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.why: Near misses reveal the same weaknesses that lead to accidents, without the harm.

RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.q: After corrective actions are implemented, the company should:
options: Check that the actions are effective
RAIA - Risk Assessment, Incident Investi.why: Verifying effectiveness confirms that the risk has really been reduced.

RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.q: What is the first step in a risk assessment?
RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.why: You cannot assess or control risks until the hazards have been identified.

options: A table combining likelihood and consequence to rate risk
RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.why: A risk matrix rates each risk by combining how likely and how severe it is.

RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.q: When there are many risks, which should be dealt with first?
RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.why: Prioritizing the highest risks reduces the greatest potential harm first.

RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.q: What does ALARP mean in risk management?
RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.why: ALARP means reducing risk as far as is reasonably practicable.

RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.q: Replacing a toxic cleaning chemical with a safer one is an example of:
RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.why: Substitution replaces a hazardous material or process with a less hazardous one.

RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.q: Why should risk assessments be recorded?
options: So controls can be communicated, reused and reviewed
RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.why: Written assessments let the team share, reuse and review the agreed controls.

options: How often the task is done
How serious the harm would be
How many people are on board
RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.why: Severity is the seriousness of the harm if the hazard results in an incident.

RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.q: Before changing equipment, procedures or crew arrangements, the safety management system normally requires:
options: Making the change first and assessing later
A management of change process with risk assessment
RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.why: Management of change makes sure new risks from a change are assessed before it is made.

RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.q: What is a dynamic risk assessment?
options: Continuous checking of risks during the task as conditions change
A risk assessment done once a year
An assessment done only in port
RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.why: Conditions on board change, so risks must be watched and reassessed while the work goes on.

RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.q: If a crew member sees that a job has become unsafe, he should:
options: Use his stop-work authority and inform the officer in charge
Wait until the job is finished
RAM - Risk Assessment and Management.why: Stop-work authority lets anyone halt unsafe work until the risk is controlled.

options: Relying only on the master's experience
Effective use of all bridge resources, including people, equipment and information
RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.why: BRM is the effective management and use of all available resources to achieve a safe voyage.

options: A sequence of small errors that can lead to an accident
A list of officers on watch
RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.why: Accidents usually follow a chain of errors, and breaking any link can prevent them.

RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.q: When a pilot is on board, responsibility for the safety of the ship:
options: Remains with the master and OOW, who must monitor the pilot
RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.why: The pilot advises, but the master and OOW remain responsible and must monitor the pilot's actions.

RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.q: If the OOW sees the master making a navigational error, the OOW should:
options: Write it in a private notebook
Speak up clearly and question the action
RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.why: Challenge and response helps catch errors, whatever the rank of the person making them.

RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.q: Why is a bridge team briefing held before entering port?
options: So everyone shares the same plan and knows their role
RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.why: A briefing creates a shared understanding of the plan, roles and possible dangers.

RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.q: Cross-checking navigational information by another team member helps to:
options: Detect errors before they cause harm
RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.why: A second person checking reduces the chance that a single person's error goes unnoticed.

RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.q: The OOW should call the master when:
options: Only at the end of the watch
In any doubt, or when the standing orders require it
RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.why: STCW watchkeeping principles and standing orders require the OOW to call the master whenever in doubt.

RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.q: Which human factor most reduces a watchkeeper's alertness on night watches?
RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.why: Fatigue lowers alertness and slows reactions, especially during night watches.

options: Clear standard phrases, such as the IMO SMCP, with confirmation
RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.why: Standard phrases with confirmation reduce misunderstanding in a multinational bridge team.

RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.q: Over-reliance on automation such as ECDIS and autopilot can lead to:
RBTMBRM - Refresher for BRM and BTM.why: Trusting automation too much can make the team stop monitoring and cross-checking.

options: The reduction in under-keel clearance when a ship moves through shallow water
The rolling of a ship in heavy seas
RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.why: Squat is the bodily sinkage and trim change of a moving ship, which reduces under-keel clearance.
Squat increases rapidly with speed, so reducing speed is the main way to control it.

RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.q: On a ship with a single right-handed fixed-pitch propeller, when going astern the stern usually moves to:
RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.why: A right-handed propeller turning astern usually pulls the stern to port, so the bow swings to starboard.

RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.q: When a ship moves close to and parallel with a bank in a channel, the usual effect is:
options: The whole ship is pushed away from the bank
The stern is drawn towards the bank and the bow pushed away
RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.why: Bank effect sucks the stern towards the bank and pushes the bow away, which can cause a sheer.

RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.q: To reduce dangerous interaction when passing close to another ship in a narrow channel, ships should:
RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.why: Interaction forces increase with speed, so lower speed reduces the risk.

RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.q: When a ship is moving ahead, its pivot point is usually located:
options: Exactly at midships at all times
RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.why: When moving ahead, the pivot point moves forward of midships, roughly a quarter to a third of the length from the bow.

RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.q: Why is rudder effect poor when the engine is stopped at low speed?
options: There is little water flowing past the rudder
RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.why: A rudder needs water flow to create a turning force, and flow is weak at low speed with no propeller wash.

RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.q: When berthing, heading into the current is usually preferred because:
options: It makes the ship go faster
It always removes the need for tugs
It gives better control at low speed over the ground
RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.why: Stemming the current keeps water flowing past the rudder while the ship moves slowly over the ground.

RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.q: In shallow water, a ship's turning circle generally:
RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.why: Shallow water increases resistance to turning, so the turning circle becomes larger.

RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.q: When approaching an anchorage, the ship should:
options: Approach slowly, heading into the wind or current
Approach stern first in strong wind
Drop the anchor while turning at full speed
RCSHM - Refresher Course on Ship Handlin.why: A slow approach into the wind or current gives control and reduces strain on the anchor and cable.

RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.why: CPA is the closest distance a target will come to own ship if both keep their course and speed.

options: Time to Closest Point of Approach
RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.why: TCPA is the time remaining until the target reaches its closest point of approach.

RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.q: According to COLREG Rule 7, risk of collision should be considered to exist if:
options: The target is on the starboard quarter
The compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not change appreciably
The target shows a white light
RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.why: A steady bearing with decreasing range is the classic sign of risk of collision.

RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.q: Under COLREG Rule 7, assumptions about risk of collision must not be made on the basis of:
RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.why: Rule 7 specifically warns against assumptions based on scanty, especially scanty radar, information.

RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.q: ARPA true vectors of targets will be wrong if:
options: Own ship's speed or heading input is incorrect
The range rings are switched off
The radar is in colour mode
RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.why: ARPA calculates true target motion from own ship's heading and speed, so wrong inputs give wrong results.

RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.q: The ARPA trial maneuver function is used to:
options: Test the result of a planned course or speed change before making it
RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.why: A trial maneuver shows the predicted CPA of targets if the planned action is taken.

RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.q: On relative vectors, a target whose vector points directly at own ship indicates:
RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.why: A relative vector through own ship's position means the CPA is near zero.

RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.q: In restricted visibility, a vessel detected by radar alone is forward of the beam and a close-quarters situation is developing. Own ship should avoid:
options: An alteration of course to starboard
An alteration of course to port, unless overtaking that vessel
RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.why: COLREG Rule 19(d) says to avoid altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam, other than one being overtaken.

RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.q: Under COLREG Rule 8, action to avoid collision should be:
options: Large enough to be readily apparent to the other vessel
A series of small course changes
RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.why: Rule 8 requires bold action that is readily apparent, and warns against a succession of small alterations.

RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.q: When two tracked targets pass very close to each other, ARPA may:
options: Swap the tracking data between them
RNRPUA - Radar Navigation, Radar Plottin.why: Target swap can happen when echoes merge, so the operator must check the data after targets pass close.

ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.q: On a relative motion radar display, own ship:
options: Stays at a fixed point while targets move relative to it
Moves across the screen at its true speed
ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.why: In relative motion, own ship is fixed and targets show their motion relative to own ship.

ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.q: Why are radar plots often taken at 6-minute intervals?
options: Because radar updates only every 6 minutes
Because distance run in 6 minutes is one-tenth of the speed in knots
Because the gyro updates every 6 minutes
ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.why: Six minutes is one-tenth of an hour, which makes speed and distance calculations easy.

ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.q: In the radar plotting triangle (OAW), the line WA represents:
options: The relative motion of the target
The target's true course and speed
ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.why: WA is the target's true vector, found by combining own ship's motion (WO) and relative motion (OA).

ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.q: How is the CPA found on a manual radar plot?
options: By measuring the target's first range
By measuring the bearing change only
By using own ship's speed only
By extending the relative motion line and measuring its closest distance to own ship
ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.why: The closest distance from own ship to the extended relative motion line is the CPA.

ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.q: A target's bearing remains steady while its range decreases. This means:
options: There is a risk of collision
ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.why: A steady bearing with closing range shows the target is on a collision course.

ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.q: Under COLREG Rule 6, vessels using radar must consider, when deciding a safe speed:
options: The characteristics, efficiency and limitations of the radar equipment
ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.why: Rule 6 lists radar limitations among the factors for safe speed for vessels with operational radar.

ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.q: On a relative motion display, a stationary object such as a buoy appears to move:
options: In the same direction as own ship
Opposite to own ship's course, at own ship's speed
ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.why: Because own ship is fixed on the display, stationary objects move at own speed in the reciprocal direction.

ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.q: Under COLREG Rule 8, action to avoid collision should be taken:
options: Only after the other vessel acts
In ample time and with due regard to good seamanship
ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.why: Rule 8 requires action to be positive, made in ample time and with good seamanship.

ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.q: The time to CPA (TCPA) is found from:
options: The distance along the relative motion line to CPA, divided by the relative speed
The radar range scale in use
ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.why: TCPA is how long the target takes to travel along its relative track to the CPA.

ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.q: Under COLREG Rule 19, a vessel that hears the fog signal of another vessel apparently forward of her beam should, unless no risk of collision exists:
options: Reduce speed to the minimum at which she can keep her course
ROPA - Radar Observation and Plotting.why: Rule 19(e) requires reducing speed to the minimum for steering, and taking all way off if necessary.

RSDI - Rightship Inspection.q: RightShip inspections are most commonly requested for which type of vessel?
RSDI - Rightship Inspection.why: RightShip vetting and inspection are mainly used by charterers to assess dry bulk carriers.

RSDI - Rightship Inspection.q: What does RISQ stand for in RightShip inspections?
RSDI - Rightship Inspection.why: RISQ is the RightShip Inspection Ship Questionnaire that the inspector follows on board.

RSDI - Rightship Inspection.q: Why do charterers and cargo owners use RightShip vetting?
options: To set the crew's wage scale
To choose the cheapest bunker supplier
To decide the ship's flag of registry
To reduce the risk of chartering a substandard ship
RSDI - Rightship Inspection.why: Vetting helps charterers avoid ships with safety or quality risks.

RSDI - Rightship Inspection.q: On the RightShip platform, the Safety Score ranges from 1 to 5. Which score shows the lowest risk?
RSDI - Rightship Inspection.why: The RightShip Safety Score runs from 1 to 5, with 5 being the best (lowest risk).

RSDI - Rightship Inspection.q: What is the best way for the ship to prepare before a RightShip inspection?
options: Hide records that show past defects
Do an internal check using the inspection questionnaire
Ask the crew to stay in their cabins
Postpone all maintenance until after the visit
RSDI - Rightship Inspection.why: A self-check against the questionnaire finds gaps early so they can be corrected honestly.

RSDI - Rightship Inspection.q: During the inspection, the inspector asks a crew member how to start the emergency fire pump. What should the crew member do?
options: Refer the inspector to the agent
Say it is not his job and walk away
Guess the answer to save time
Explain or demonstrate the correct procedure
RSDI - Rightship Inspection.why: Inspectors check observable practice, so crew must be able to show they know their duties.

RSDI - Rightship Inspection.q: Which documents should be checked as part of preparation?
options: Ship certificates, records and logs for validity and consistency
Only the crew's personal travel documents
Only the menu and provision list
RSDI - Rightship Inspection.why: Valid certificates and consistent records are a key part of any inspection.

RSDI - Rightship Inspection.q: What does a RightShip inspector mainly compare during the visit?
options: The ship's speed with other ships
The crew's salaries with industry rates
What the records say with what is actually done on board
The ship's age with its purchase price
RSDI - Rightship Inspection.why: Inspections verify that real practices match the documented procedures and records.

RSDI - Rightship Inspection.q: After the inspection, how should identified observations or gaps be handled?
options: Ignore them until the next inspection
Delete them from the ship's records
Blame the inspector for the findings
Find the root cause, correct them and send evidence of close-out
RSDI - Rightship Inspection.why: Proper follow-up means root cause analysis, corrective action and proof that the gap is closed.

RSDI - Rightship Inspection.q: What attitude should the crew show toward the inspector?
RSDI - Rightship Inspection.why: Honest and professional cooperation gives a true picture of the ship and builds trust.

options: A disease caught from other people
The body and mind's response to pressure or demands
A sign that a person is weak
A condition that only affects officers
SAM - Stress and Anger Management.why: Stress is the natural physical and mental reaction to demands or pressure.

options: A medicine used to calm anger
A rule in the ship's safety plan
A situation or event that sets off a person's anger
SAM - Stress and Anger Management.why: Triggers are the events, words or situations that start an anger reaction.

SAM - Stress and Anger Management.q: When you feel anger rising during an argument, what is a good first step?
options: Pause and take slow, deep breaths
Raise your voice to win the argument
Leave your post without telling anyone
SAM - Stress and Anger Management.why: Pausing and breathing slowly calms the body before you respond.

SAM - Stress and Anger Management.q: Which of these is an example of an 'I' statement?
options: You always make mistakes on watch
I feel upset when orders are not repeated back
SAM - Stress and Anger Management.why: An 'I' statement expresses your feelings without blaming the other person.

options: The body's automatic reaction to face or escape a threat
A method for settling disputes in court
A rule for choosing a work partner
SAM - Stress and Anger Management.why: Fight-or-flight is the body's natural alarm reaction that prepares it to face or run from danger.

SAM - Stress and Anger Management.q: Which is a common physical sign of anger?
options: Clenched fists and a faster heartbeat
SAM - Stress and Anger Management.why: Anger activates the body, causing tense muscles and a faster heart rate.

options: Waiting for your turn to speak
Giving full attention and checking you understood
SAM - Stress and Anger Management.why: Active listening means focusing on the speaker and confirming what they meant.

SAM - Stress and Anger Management.q: You have a conflict with a crewmate. What is the most constructive action?
options: Talk calmly in private and involve a superior if needed
Refuse to work with the crewmate
Wait for a chance to get even
SAM - Stress and Anger Management.why: Calm private discussion, with escalation if unresolved, solves conflict without harm.

options: Stepping away briefly to calm down, then returning to talk
Stopping work for the rest of the day
Ignoring the other person for a week
SAM - Stress and Anger Management.why: A short time-out lets emotions settle so the issue can be discussed calmly.

SAM - Stress and Anger Management.q: Why is drinking alcohol a poor way to manage stress or anger onboard?
options: It is allowed at any time on duty
It can worsen mood, judgment and safety
SAM - Stress and Anger Management.why: Alcohol impairs judgment and self-control and increases the risk of conflict and accidents.

SARTA - SART Awareness.why: SART means Search and Rescue Transponder, a GMDSS locating device.

SARTA - SART Awareness.q: A radar SART responds to which type of radar?
SARTA - SART Awareness.why: A radar SART operates in the 9 GHz X-band and answers X-band radar pulses.

SARTA - SART Awareness.q: How does a radar SART appear on a rescue ship's radar screen when it is several miles away?
options: As a line of 12 dots extending outward from the SART position
As a single large circle around own ship
As text showing the vessel name
SARTA - SART Awareness.why: At a distance the SART response shows as a line of 12 dots, with the nearest dot marking its position.

SARTA - SART Awareness.q: What is the main purpose of a SART?
options: To send weather reports to shore
To communicate by voice with other ships
To help rescue units locate the survival craft
SARTA - SART Awareness.why: The SART's locating signal guides searching ships and aircraft to the survivors.

SARTA - SART Awareness.q: A SART battery must last for 96 hours on standby and then how long while transmitting?
SARTA - SART Awareness.why: IMO standards require 96 hours standby followed by 8 hours of transmission when interrogated.

SARTA - SART Awareness.q: For good detection range, a radar SART should be mounted at least how high above sea level?
SARTA - SART Awareness.why: IMO standards are based on the SART being at least 1 metre above sea level; higher gives better range.

SARTA - SART Awareness.q: When abandoning ship, what should be done with the SART?
options: Take it to the survival craft and switch it on
Leave it in its bracket on the bridge
Throw it into the sea away from the craft
Keep it switched off until land is seen
SARTA - SART Awareness.why: The SART is carried into the survival craft and activated so rescuers can find it.

SARTA - SART Awareness.q: What is an important precaution when testing a SART on board?
options: Test it for as long as possible
Test it only while in the water
Test briefly using own radar to avoid false alerts
SARTA - SART Awareness.why: Short tests avoid other ships mistaking the signal for a real distress.

SARTA - SART Awareness.q: How does an AIS-SART show its position to rescue units?
options: By flashing a strobe light only
By transmitting its GPS position over AIS
By sending a voice message on VHF
By releasing coloured dye in the water
SARTA - SART Awareness.why: An AIS-SART sends its GPS position through AIS, which appears on AIS displays and ECDIS.

SARTA - SART Awareness.q: During routine inspection of a SART, what should the crew check?
options: The colour of the paint on the bracket
The serial number of the radar
The ship's call sign on the lanyard only
The battery expiry date and general condition
SARTA - SART Awareness.why: An expired battery or damaged unit may fail in an emergency, so these must be checked.

SDC - Smoke Diving Course.why: SCBA is the Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus worn for entry into smoke-filled spaces.

SDC - Smoke Diving Course.q: Which check is done before wearing the breathing apparatus?
options: Checking the colour of the harness
Checking cylinder pressure and the face mask seal
Checking the weight of the helmet
Checking the length of the lifeline only
SDC - Smoke Diving Course.why: Adequate air pressure and a tight mask seal are essential before entering smoke.

SDC - Smoke Diving Course.q: What should the wearer do when the low-pressure warning whistle sounds?
options: Remove the face mask to save air
Wait for the whistle to stop
SDC - Smoke Diving Course.why: The whistle warns that air is running low, so the wearer must leave at once.

SDC - Smoke Diving Course.q: Why should smoke divers always work in pairs?
options: So they can help each other and stay safe
So one can carry extra tools
Because the rules require a race
SDC - Smoke Diving Course.why: Working in pairs means a partner can assist or raise the alarm if something goes wrong.

SDC - Smoke Diving Course.q: In rope signals between the smoke diver and the attendant, what do four pulls mean?
SDC - Smoke Diving Course.why: In the common OATH system, four pulls mean Help.

SDC - Smoke Diving Course.q: How should you move inside a compartment with zero visibility?
options: Run quickly to find the exit
Stay low and feel ahead with your hand or foot
SDC - Smoke Diving Course.why: Moving low and testing ahead protects you from heat, openings and obstacles.

SDC - Smoke Diving Course.q: Why is it safer to stay low in a smoke-filled space?
options: The floor is always cooler metal
Rescuers only search near the floor
Heat and smoke rise, so it is cooler and clearer below
SDC - Smoke Diving Course.why: Hot gases and smoke rise, leaving cooler air and better visibility near the deck.

SDC - Smoke Diving Course.q: What search technique helps divers not get lost in a dark compartment?
options: Keeping contact with a wall and with the partner
Following the sound of the engines
SDC - Smoke Diving Course.why: Wall-contact search and partner contact give a fixed reference for the way back.

SDC - Smoke Diving Course.q: Before opening a door to a possible fire area, how should you check it?
options: Open it quickly to look inside
Kick it to test its strength
Feel the door with the back of your hand
SDC - Smoke Diving Course.why: Checking the door with the back of the hand detects heat behind it without burning your palm.

SDC - Smoke Diving Course.q: What does the entry control officer record when a team enters with breathing apparatus?
options: Names, entry time and cylinder pressure
SDC - Smoke Diving Course.why: These records let the control officer calculate safe working time and track who is inside.

SGS - Ship General Safety.q: What is the main purpose of the ISM Code?
options: To set crew wages and contracts
To ensure safety at sea and prevent pollution
SGS - Ship General Safety.why: The ISM Code provides an international standard for safe ship management and pollution prevention.

SGS - Ship General Safety.q: What is the general emergency alarm signal on board?
options: Seven or more short blasts followed by one long blast
One short and one long blast repeated
SGS - Ship General Safety.why: SOLAS sets the general alarm as seven or more short blasts followed by one long blast.

SGS - Ship General Safety.q: What does the muster list show?
options: Each person's emergency duties and muster station
SGS - Ship General Safety.why: The muster list assigns emergency duties and stations and is posted in conspicuous places.

options: An accident that caused serious injury
A ship passing close to land
An event that could have caused harm but did not
SGS - Ship General Safety.why: A near miss is an unplanned event with potential for harm that should be reported to prevent accidents.

SGS - Ship General Safety.q: Under SOLAS, how often should each crew member take part in an abandon ship drill?
SGS - Ship General Safety.why: SOLAS requires each crew member to take part in at least one abandon ship drill every month.

SGS - Ship General Safety.q: What is the purpose of lockout/tagout before maintenance?
options: To isolate energy sources so equipment cannot start
SGS - Ship General Safety.why: Lockout/tagout prevents accidental start-up or release of energy while work is done.

SGS - Ship General Safety.q: Who is the Designated Person Ashore (DPA)?
options: The link between the ship and the highest level of company management
The port agent who handles cargo documents
The crewing officer who hires seafarers
SGS - Ship General Safety.why: Under the ISM Code, the DPA provides a direct link between the ship and top management.

SGS - Ship General Safety.q: Which work normally needs a permit to work?
SGS - Ship General Safety.why: High-risk jobs like hot work require a permit to control hazards.

SGS - Ship General Safety.q: What is the main purpose of personal protective equipment (PPE)?
options: To protect the worker from remaining hazards
SGS - Ship General Safety.why: PPE is the last line of defence against hazards that cannot be removed by other controls.

SGS - Ship General Safety.q: You see a fire in a store room. What should you do first?
options: Open all doors to let smoke out
SGS - Ship General Safety.why: Raising the alarm first brings help and starts the emergency response.

options: The ship rising out of the water at high speed
The ship listing due to wind
The ship sinking bodily and changing trim when moving in shallow water
The ship drifting sideways at anchor
SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.why: Squat is the increase in draft and change of trim caused by speed in shallow water.

SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.q: What is the most effective way to reduce squat?
SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.why: Squat increases roughly with the square of speed, so slowing down reduces it the most.

SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.q: A ship with a right-handed fixed-pitch propeller goes astern. Which way does the stern usually swing?
SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.why: Transverse thrust from a right-handed propeller going astern pushes the stern to port.

SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.q: What is the tactical diameter of a ship?
options: The distance travelled during a crash stop
The transfer when the ship has turned 180 degrees
SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.why: Tactical diameter is the sideways distance covered when the heading has changed by 180 degrees.

SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.q: When moving ahead, the pivot point is usually located where?
options: About one-quarter to one-third of the length from the bow
At the stern near the rudder
Outside the ship ahead of the bow
SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.why: With headway the pivot point moves forward to roughly a quarter to a third of the length from the bow.

SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.q: When a ship runs close to a channel bank, what usually happens?
options: The whole ship is pushed away from the bank
The ship speeds up and lifts
The stern is drawn toward the bank and the bow sheers away
SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.why: Bank effect causes stern suction toward the bank and a bow cushion that pushes the bow away.

SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.q: Why is rudder effect poor at very low speed with the engine stopped?
options: Little water flows past the rudder
SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.why: A rudder needs water flow over it; a short kick ahead increases the flow and steering effect.

SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.q: Where on the bridge can the officer find the ship's turning and stopping data?
options: On the wheelhouse poster and manoeuvring booklet
SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.why: IMO guidance requires manoeuvring information such as the wheelhouse poster to be on the bridge.

SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.q: Two ships pass close in a narrow channel. What is the main risk?
SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.why: Pressure fields between close ships cause suction and sheering, so speed and distance must be managed.

SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.q: What is the safest general approach when berthing?
options: Slow speed, a planned approach angle, and allowance for wind and current
High speed to keep good steering
Approaching parallel to the berth at full ahead
Ignoring the tide because the berth is sheltered
SHM - Ship Handling and Maneuvering.why: Controlled low speed and planning for wind and current reduce the risk of heavy contact.

SMC - Stress Management Course.q: Under the STCW and MLC rules, what is the minimum rest a seafarer must have in any 24-hour period?
SMC - Stress Management Course.why: STCW and MLC require at least 10 hours of rest in any 24-hour period.

SMC - Stress Management Course.q: What is the minimum rest required in any 7-day period?
SMC - Stress Management Course.why: The minimum rest is 77 hours in any 7-day period.

SMC - Stress Management Course.q: Which is a common cause of fatigue on board?
options: Long working hours and poor sleep
SMC - Stress Management Course.why: Long hours and broken or poor sleep are leading causes of seafarer fatigue.

SMC - Stress Management Course.q: How does fatigue affect a seafarer's work?
options: It has no effect on safety
It slows reactions and increases mistakes
SMC - Stress Management Course.why: Fatigue reduces attention and reaction time, increasing the chance of errors and accidents.

SMC - Stress Management Course.q: Which is a healthy coping technique for stress?
options: Staying awake to finish more work
SMC - Stress Management Course.why: Exercise and controlled breathing reduce stress hormones and calm the body.

SMC - Stress Management Course.q: Which is a common sign that a person is under too much stress?
SMC - Stress Management Course.why: Irritability, poor concentration and sleep problems are typical signs of stress.

SMC - Stress Management Course.q: You notice a crewmate has become quiet and withdrawn. What should you do?
options: Ignore it because it is personal
Tell everyone about it at mealtime
Talk to them kindly and encourage them to seek help
SMC - Stress Management Course.why: Peer support means noticing changes and helping the person reach support early.

SMC - Stress Management Course.q: What helps improve sleep before rest periods?
options: Eating a heavy meal right before sleeping
A dark, quiet cabin and limiting caffeine
SMC - Stress Management Course.why: A quiet, dark environment and less caffeine help the body get quality sleep.

SMC - Stress Management Course.q: How can good time management reduce workload stress?
options: By doing all tasks at the same time
By leaving tasks to the last minute
By skipping rest to finish early
SMC - Stress Management Course.why: Planning and prioritising tasks keeps work under control and reduces pressure.

SMC - Stress Management Course.q: If stress becomes too much to handle alone, what is the best action?
options: Hide it to avoid looking weak
Speak with a superior, the medical officer or a welfare helpline
SMC - Stress Management Course.why: Seeking support early from trusted people or welfare services protects health and safety.

options: A storage area for spare ropes
The place where the pilot boards
The area where a parted line may recoil violently
SMO - Safe Mooring Operations.why: When a loaded line parts, it can whip back with great force through the snap-back zone.

SMO - Safe Mooring Operations.q: Why should crew not rely only on painted snap-back zone markings?
options: The markings show where lines are stored
A parted line can recoil outside the painted area
The markings are only for decoration
SMO - Safe Mooring Operations.why: Snap-back paths are hard to predict, so the whole mooring area must be treated as hazardous.

SMO - Safe Mooring Operations.q: What does the ship's mooring plan show?
options: The arrangement of lines, leads and equipment for mooring
SMO - Safe Mooring Operations.why: The mooring plan shows how lines are led and which equipment to use.

SMO - Safe Mooring Operations.q: What is the main rule about standing near ropes during mooring?
options: Stand in the bight to guide the rope
Never stand in the bight of a rope or in the line of fire
Sit on the bitts to save energy
Hold the rope with bare hands near the drum
SMO - Safe Mooring Operations.why: Standing in a bight or line of fire can lead to serious injury if the rope moves or parts.

SMO - Safe Mooring Operations.q: Why should mooring lines be tended while alongside?
